title: Bhairava at the door
hook: Brahma boasts, and in an instant a fierce form springs out of Shiva: Bhairava, who now guards Kashi
carry: bhairava is the flash that cuts the ego

segments.voice: Yesterday: the teacher is the way, and a minister who met Shiva under a tree. Today, Shiva's fiercest face, and a line in the Shiva Sutras that names him.
screen: `GURUR UPAYAH.` · `TODAY: THE ONE AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Brahma, the creator, is boasting. In the Shiva Purana's telling, he grows so proud that he speaks of Shiva with contempt, as if he himself were the source of everything. And in an instant, faster than an argument, a figure springs out of Shiva: dark, fierce, eyes blazing. Bhairava. He goes straight to Brahma and, with one fingernail, cuts off the head that boasted. Brahma had five heads. From that day, the story says, he has four.
screen: `BRAHMA BOASTS.` → `IN AN INSTANT, BHAIRAVA.` → `FIVE HEADS, THEN FOUR.`

segments.voice: The story keeps going. The skull sticks to Bhairava's hand. Even a god who cuts down pride has to answer for the cut, so Bhairava wanders the world as a beggar, the skull for his bowl, until he reaches Kashi, the city of Varanasi. There it falls from his hand. Shiva makes him Kashi's guardian, and pilgrims in Varanasi still visit Kala Bhairava; many Shiva temples keep a shrine to Bhairava too, a fierce figure with a dog. Many teachers read the fifth head as ahamkara, the ego, the I that boasts. Bhairava is Shiva's answer to it: not a lecture, a flash. Now the Shiva Sutras use his name: udyamo bhairavah. Udyama is an upsurge, a springing up. The upsurge is Bhairava. Commentators read it as the sudden flash of awareness, consciousness springing up all at once, not reasoned into step by step. In Kashmir Shaivism, Bhairava isn't only a fierce figure near the door. He's a name for consciousness itself, awake. And the flash, as in the story, cuts the boasting head: the little I that thought it was the center of everything. Here's how it meets an ordinary day. You're halfway through an argument, or a daydream, or a brag, and suddenly you see yourself doing it. That snap, before the next thought, isn't your failure. On this teaching, it's Bhairava at the door.
screen: `THE SKULL FALLS IN KASHI.` · `THE FIFTH HEAD: THE EGO.` · `UDYAMO BHAIRAVAH: THE UPSURGE.` · `CONSCIOUSNESS, AWAKE, IS BHAIRAVA.` · then, large: `THE FLASH THAT CUTS THE BOAST.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on the breath, and when the mind wanders off, as it will, don't scold it. Pause in the noticing itself, that snap of being awake again, for one breath. Then return, and wait for the next one. If you pray, greet each return with Om namah shivaya, or with Bhairava's name. If you don't, let the snap be the whole practice.
Udyamo bhairavah. The upsurge is Bhairava: the sudden flash of awareness, Shiva's fierce form, cutting the boasting I.
Your line: Bhairava is the flash that cuts the ego. The snap of seeing yourself is the point, not the mistake. Until tomorrow.
